# Logistic Regression for Classification

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
Logistic regression, maximum likelihood, and probabilistic classification are developed in greater depth in Chapters 3, 6, and 11 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Chapter objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to:

- fit a logistic-regression model for a binary response;
- interpret probabilities, coefficients, and odds ratios;
- separate probability estimation from threshold-based decision making;
- construct a confusion matrix and compute basic classification metrics;
- interpret AUC as a measure of discrimination;
- examine calibration using predicted probabilities and observed frequencies;
- apply the model to ATUS and COVID-19 while maintaining responsible interpretation.

## Mathematical foundation

Logistic regression models a probability through

$$
p(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},
$$

where

$$
z=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p.
$$

The expression on the left is the *logit* of the probability. Coefficients are commonly estimated by maximum likelihood [@cox1958regression; @hosmer2013applied].

## Logistic function

```{r logistic-function-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
library(ggplot2)
source("../util_graficas.R")

z <- seq(-10, 10, length.out = 200)
logistic_data <- data.frame(
  z = z,
  p = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
)

ggplot(logistic_data, aes(x = z, y = p)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = col_azul) +
  labs(
    title = "Logistic function",
    subtitle = "Maps real-valued scores to probabilities",
    x = "z",
    y = "Probability"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Interpretation"}
The logistic curve has an S shape. Very negative linear-predictor values produce probabilities near zero, while very positive values produce probabilities near one.
:::

# Applied Case A: ATUS

## Load and prepare the data

```{r load-atus-logistic-en}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

atus_path <- "../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv"

if (!file.exists(atus_path)) {
  stop("../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv was not found. Run the data-preparation chapter first.")
}

atus_ml <- read_csv(
  atus_path,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

atus_model <- atus_ml |>
  mutate(
    victims_binary = ifelse(
      accidente_con_victimas == "Con víctimas",
      1,
      0
    ),
    MES = as.factor(MES),
    HOUR_NUM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ID_HORA)),
    HOUR_NUM = ifelse(
      HOUR_NUM >= 0 & HOUR_NUM <= 23,
      HOUR_NUM,
      NA_real_
    ),
    DIASEMANA = as.factor(DIASEMANA),
    TIPACCID = as.factor(TIPACCID),
    CAUSAACCI = as.factor(CAUSAACCI),
    accident_class = factor(
      accidente_con_victimas,
      levels = c("Con víctimas", "Solo daños"),
      labels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only")
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(
    victims_binary,
    MES,
    HOUR_NUM,
    DIASEMANA,
    TIPACCID,
    CAUSAACCI
  )
```

::: {.callout-note title="Valid hour values"}
Hour codes outside the interval 0–23 are converted to `NA` before modeling. This avoids treating special codes as if they represented actual clock hours.
:::

## Stratified training-test split

A stratified split preserves approximately the same class proportion in training and test data.

```{r split-atus-logistic-en}
set.seed(2026)

idx_victims <- which(atus_model$victims_binary == 1)
idx_damage <- which(atus_model$victims_binary == 0)

train_victims <- sample(
  idx_victims,
  size = floor(0.70 * length(idx_victims))
)

train_damage <- sample(
  idx_damage,
  size = floor(0.70 * length(idx_damage))
)

idx_train <- sort(c(train_victims, train_damage))

train <- atus_model[idx_train, ]
test <- atus_model[-idx_train, ]

prop.table(table(train$victims_binary))
prop.table(table(test$victims_binary))
```

## Fit the model

```{r fit-atus-logistic-en}
model_logit <- glm(
  victims_binary ~ MES + HOUR_NUM + DIASEMANA + TIPACCID + CAUSAACCI,
  data = train,
  family = binomial
)

head(summary(model_logit)$coefficients, 12)
```

## Interpret coefficients and odds ratios

A coefficient $\beta_j$ represents a change in log-odds while the remaining predictors are held constant. Its exponential,

$$
OR_j=e^{\beta_j},
$$

is an odds ratio.

```{r odds-ratios-atus-en}
coef_atus <- coef(model_logit)

data.frame(
  term = names(coef_atus),
  beta = as.numeric(coef_atus),
  odds_ratio = exp(as.numeric(coef_atus))
) |>
  head(12)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="An odds ratio is not a probability ratio"}
An odds ratio should not be translated directly as “times more likely.” The relationship between odds and probability depends on the baseline probability.
:::

## Predicted probabilities and classification threshold

```{r probabilities-threshold-atus-en}
test$prob_victims <- predict(
  model_logit,
  newdata = test,
  type = "response"
)

threshold <- 0.30

test$predicted_class <- factor(
  ifelse(
    test$prob_victims >= threshold,
    "With casualties",
    "Property damage only"
  ),
  levels = c("With casualties", "Property damage only")
)
```

::: {.callout-note title="The threshold is not part of the probability model"}
Logistic regression produces probabilities. The threshold is a later decision rule. Lower thresholds usually increase sensitivity and reduce specificity; higher thresholds usually do the opposite.
:::

## Confusion matrix and metrics

```{r metrics-logistic-atus-en}
confusion_matrix <- table(
  Actual = test$accident_class,
  Predicted = test$predicted_class
)

confusion_matrix

TP <- confusion_matrix["With casualties", "With casualties"]
FN <- confusion_matrix["With casualties", "Property damage only"]
FP <- confusion_matrix["Property damage only", "With casualties"]
TN <- confusion_matrix["Property damage only", "Property damage only"]

safe_divide <- function(a, b) {
  if (b == 0) NA_real_ else a / b
}

data.frame(
  accuracy = safe_divide(TP + TN, TP + FN + FP + TN),
  sensitivity = safe_divide(TP, TP + FN),
  specificity = safe_divide(TN, TN + FP),
  precision = safe_divide(TP, TP + FP)
)
```

## Distribution of predicted probabilities

```{r probability-distribution-atus-en, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8}
ggplot(
  test,
  aes(x = prob_victims, fill = accident_class)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    alpha = 0.65,
    position = "identity"
  ) +
  escala_clases_fill(name = "Actual class") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = threshold, linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of predicted probabilities",
    subtitle = paste("Classification threshold =", threshold),
    x = "Predicted probability of an accident with casualties",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

## Discrimination: AUC

Discrimination measures how well the model ranks observations from lower to higher event probability. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarizes this ranking ability [@fawcett2006roc].

AUC can be calculated without additional packages using probability ranks:

```{r auc-logistic-atus-en}
auc_by_ranks <- function(y, prob) {
  n1 <- sum(y == 1)
  n0 <- sum(y == 0)

  if (n1 == 0 || n0 == 0) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }

  ranks <- rank(prob, ties.method = "average")

  (sum(ranks[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) /
    (n1 * n0)
}

auc_atus <- auc_by_ranks(
  test$victims_binary,
  test$prob_victims
)

auc_atus
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Interpreting AUC"}
An AUC near 0.5 indicates discrimination close to random ranking. Larger values indicate better ranking ability. AUC alone does not tell us whether the predicted probabilities are well calibrated.
:::

## Calibration

Calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed event frequencies. We group predictions into ten approximately equal-sized groups.

```{r calibration-logistic-atus-en}
calibration_atus <- test |>
  mutate(
    probability_group = ntile(prob_victims, 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(probability_group) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_probability = mean(prob_victims),
    observed_frequency = mean(victims_binary),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

calibration_atus
```

```{r calibration-plot-atus-en, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
ggplot(
  calibration_atus,
  aes(x = mean_probability, y = observed_frequency)
) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Calibration by probability groups",
    subtitle = "The diagonal represents perfect calibration",
    x = "Mean predicted probability",
    y = "Observed frequency"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Discrimination and calibration answer different questions"}
A model may rank observations well and achieve a useful AUC while systematically producing probabilities that are too high or too low. This is why discrimination and calibration should be assessed separately.
:::

# Applied Case B: COVID-19

## Select the same period used in previous chapters

```{r select-covid-logistic-en}
covid_counts <- read_csv(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

covid_year <- covid_counts |>
  filter(
    ESTADO == "PROCESADO",
    !is.na(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS)
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    CASOS_CONFIRMADOS,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(ANIO)

covid_path <- file.path(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  paste0("covid19_mexico_", covid_year, "_ml_preparado.csv.gz")
)

if (!file.exists(covid_path)) {
  stop("The COVID-19 dataset selected by the reproducible procedure was not found.")
}

covid <- read_csv(
  covid_path,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

message("COVID-19 period used: ", covid_year)
```

## Prepare the educational COVID-19 model

```{r prepare-covid-logistic-en}
covid_model <- covid |>
  select(
    MURIO,
    EDAD,
    NEUMONIA,
    DIABETES,
    HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD,
    RENAL_CRONICA
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na()
```

::: {.callout-important title="Predicted probability is not automatically population risk"}
If the dataset was constructed using death over-sampling, class balancing, or another procedure that changes prevalence, raw model probabilities do not directly represent the true population frequency. A modified sample may be useful for teaching classification and comparing algorithms, but a population-risk simulator requires natural-prevalence data or appropriate weighting and calibration methods.
:::

## Fit the COVID-19 model

```{r fit-covid-logistic-en}
set.seed(2026)

idx_covid <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(covid_model)),
  size = floor(0.80 * nrow(covid_model))
)

covid_train <- covid_model[idx_covid, ]
covid_test <- covid_model[-idx_covid, ]

covid_logit <- glm(
  MURIO ~ EDAD + NEUMONIA + DIABETES +
    HIPERTENSION + OBESIDAD + RENAL_CRONICA,
  data = covid_train,
  family = binomial
)

covid_test$sample_probability <- predict(
  covid_logit,
  newdata = covid_test,
  type = "response"
)

head(summary(covid_logit)$coefficients, 10)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Educational use only"}
This model is not a diagnostic or prognostic tool. Its coefficients describe associations within the dataset and depend on the period, coverage, data quality, and sampling strategy.
:::

## Interactive laboratory: logistic regression

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Explore how the intercept, slope, and classification threshold change the estimated probability and final predicted class.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 720
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

sigmoid <- function(z) {
  1 / (1 + exp(-z))
}

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Logistic regression laboratory"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("b0", "Intercept", -10, 10, -3, step = 0.25),
      sliderInput("b1", "Slope", -5, 5, 1.2, step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("threshold", "Classification threshold", 0.05, 0.95, 0.5, step = 0.05),
      sliderInput("xnew", "New x value", -5, 10, 2.5, step = 0.1)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("curve", height = "440px"),
      verbatimTextOutput("result"),
      textOutput("interpretation")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  new_probability <- reactive({
    sigmoid(input$b0 + input$b1 * input$xnew)
  })

  output$curve <- renderPlot({
    x <- seq(-5, 10, length.out = 400)
    p <- sigmoid(input$b0 + input$b1 * x)

    plot(
      x, p,
      type = "l",
      lwd = 3,
      ylim = c(0, 1),
      xlab = "Variable x",
      ylab = "Estimated probability",
      main = "Logistic curve and threshold"
    )

    abline(h = input$threshold, lty = 2)
    abline(v = input$xnew, lty = 3)
    points(input$xnew, new_probability(), pch = 19, cex = 1.8)
    text(
      input$xnew,
      new_probability(),
      labels = paste0("  p = ", round(new_probability(), 3)),
      pos = 4
    )
  })

  output$result <- renderPrint({
    predicted_class <- ifelse(
      new_probability() >= input$threshold,
      1,
      0
    )

    cat("Logit =", round(input$b0 + input$b1 * input$xnew, 4), "\n")
    cat("Probability =", round(new_probability(), 4), "\n")
    cat("Threshold =", input$threshold, "\n")
    cat("Predicted class =", predicted_class)
  })

  output$interpretation <- renderText({
    if (new_probability() >= input$threshold) {
      "The probability exceeds the threshold, so the observation is assigned to Class 1."
    } else {
      "The probability does not reach the threshold, so the observation is assigned to Class 0."
    }
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

## Chapter summary

Logistic regression clearly separates two stages: probability estimation and, when a class is required, threshold-based assignment. Discrimination, calibration, and threshold-dependent metrics answer different questions. Responsible interpretation of probabilities requires attention to prevalence, sampling, and calibration, especially in health applications.
